'apologise' takes 'for' before the reason, not 'of'.
'apologise at' is not used for the reason.

solution: I would like to apologise for keeping you waiting.
'apologise for' + the fault.

questions.stem: Tom was accused ____ cheating, though he had done nothing wrong.

explain.why: 'accused with' is not used; 'charged with' is a different phrase.
'accused' takes 'of' before the offence, not 'for'.
'accused on' is not used for the offence.

solution: Tom was accused of cheating, though he had done nothing wrong.
'accuse someone of' + the offence.

questions.stem: Pupils must refrain ____ running along the corridors.

explain.why: 'refrain at' is not used in English.
'refrain with' is not used in English; 'refrain' takes 'from'.
'refrain to' is not used; the verb takes 'from' before a gerund.

solution: Pupils must refrain from running along the corridors.
'refrain from' + gerund.

questions.stem: Mei Ling enjoys ____ in the school choir.

explain.why: 'enjoy' is followed by a gerund (-ing), not 'to' + verb.
'sang' is a past tense and cannot follow 'enjoys'.
'enjoy' needs the -ing form; the base form 'sing' is ungrammatical here.

solution: Mei Ling enjoys singing in the school choir.
'enjoy' + gerund: enjoys singing.

questions.stem: We decided ____ the zoo on Saturday.

explain.why: 'decide' is followed by 'to' + verb, not a gerund.
'decided' must be followed by an infinitive, not a past tense.
'decide' needs 'to' before the verb.

solution: We decided to visit the zoo on Saturday.
'decide' + to-infinitive: decided to visit.

questions.stem: Jun is looking forward to ____ his grandparents.

explain.why: 'look forward to' already has 'to'; another 'to' is not added.
A preposition cannot be followed by a past tense verb.
'to' here is a preposition, so the verb after it must be -ing.

solution: Jun is looking forward to seeing his grandparents.
'look forward to' + gerund: looking forward to seeing.

questions.stem: I am tired of ____ the same food every day.

explain.why: After the preposition 'of', the verb takes -ing.
A preposition cannot be followed by a past tense verb.
'tired of' is followed by a gerund, not 'to' + verb.

solution: I am tired of eating the same food every day.
Preposition + gerund: tired of eating.

questions.stem: Would you mind ____ the window?

explain.why: 'mind' cannot be followed by a past tense verb.
'Would you mind' needs the -ing form.
'mind' is followed by a gerund, not 'to' + verb.

solution: Would you mind closing the window?
'mind' + gerund: Would you mind closing...?

questions.stem: The vase, ____ by a naughty puppy, lay in pieces on the floor.

explain.why: The base form 'break' cannot follow a noun here.
The vase was broken by the puppy, so the passive participle is needed, not -ing.
'to break' shows purpose and does not say who broke the vase.

solution: The vase, broken by a naughty puppy, lay in pieces on the floor.
A past participle gives a passive meaning: the vase, broken by a puppy.

questions.stem: My teacher made us ____ the school song three times.

explain.why: 'made us' is followed by the base verb, not -ing.
'make' someone do something takes the bare verb, without 'to'.
After 'made us' the base form is needed, not the past tense.

solution: My teacher made us sing the school song three times.
'make someone' + bare infinitive: made us sing.

questions.stem: We could not help ____ when the clown slipped on the banana skin.

explain.why: 'could not help' needs the -ing form.
'cannot help' is followed by -ing, not 'to' + verb.
'help' cannot be followed by a past tense verb.

solution: We could not help laughing when the clown slipped on the banana skin.
'cannot help' + gerund: could not help laughing.

questions.stem: Having ____ his homework, Jun Jie went out to play basketball.

explain.why: 'Having finishing' is not a correct form; 'having' takes the past participle.
'Having been finished' is passive, but Jun Jie did the finishing.
'Having' must be followed by a past participle.

solution: Having finished his homework, Jun Jie went out to play basketball.
'Having' + past participle shows the earlier action: Having finished...

questions.stem: The coach suggested ____ an extra training session before the match.

explain.why: 'suggested' cannot be followed directly by a past tense verb.
'suggest' is followed by a gerund, not 'to' + verb.
'suggested have' is wrong; 'suggest' needs the -ing form here.

solution: The coach suggested having an extra training session before the match.
'suggest' + gerund: suggested having.

questions.stem: The old shophouse, ____ in 1920, is now a museum.

explain.why: 'was built' would add a second finite verb between commas, making the sentence ungrammatical.
'build' is the base form; the passive meaning needs the past participle 'built'.
The shophouse did not build itself, so the passive participle 'built' is needed.

solution: The old shophouse, built in 1920, is now a museum.
A past participle phrase gives a passive meaning: the shophouse, built in 1920.

questions.stem: I would rather ____ in the shade than play in this heat.

explain.why: 'would rather' is followed by the bare infinitive, without 'to'.
'would rather' is followed by the base form, not the past tense, for a present preference.
'would rather' needs the base form, not -ing.

solution: I would rather sit in the shade than play in this heat.
'would rather' + bare infinitive: would rather sit.

questions.stem: Rain or shine, the hawker is used to ____ up at four in the morning.

explain.why: In 'be used to', 'to' is a preposition, so the verb must be -ing.
'used to' (be accustomed) cannot be followed by a past tense verb.
'is used to' already contains 'to'; another 'to' is not added.

solution: Rain or shine, the hawker is used to waking up at four in the morning.
'be used to' + gerund: is used to waking up.

questions.stem: Not ____ what to say, Hui Min kept quiet.

explain.why: 'Not to know' changes the meaning to a purpose and does not explain why she kept quiet.
A participle phrase at the start needs -ing, not the base form.
'known' is passive; Hui Min was the one who did not know.

solution: Not knowing what to say, Hui Min kept quiet.
A participial phrase of reason takes -ing: Not knowing...

questions.stem: The boys ____ playing football on the field.

explain.why: 'is' needs a singular subject, but the subject here is 'The boys'.
'was' goes with a singular subject, but 'The boys' is plural.
'has' cannot be followed by 'playing' as a continuous form; 'are playing' is needed.

solution: The boys are playing football on the field.
'The boys' is plural, so use 'are'.

questions.stem: Everyone in my class ____ a library card.

explain.why: 'having' is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.
'Everyone' is singular, so it takes 'has', not 'have'.
'are' cannot be followed by 'a library card' and does not agree with 'Everyone'.

solution: Everyone in my class has a library card.
'Everyone' is singular, so 'has'.

questions.stem: My brother and my sister ____ the same tuition teacher.

explain.why: 'does' is an auxiliary and does not mean 'possess' here.
Two subjects joined by 'and' make a plural subject, so 'has' is wrong.
'is' cannot link to 'the same tuition teacher' as an action verb, and it is singular.

solution: My brother and my sister have the same tuition teacher.
'My brother and my sister' is a plural subject, so 'have'.

questions.stem: The water in those bottles ____ still cold.

explain.why: 'are' agrees with the nearby 'bottles', but the subject is 'The water', which is singular.
'be' is not a finite verb and does not agree with 'The water'; 'is' is needed.
'were' is plural; the subject is 'The water'.

solution: The water in those bottles is still cold.
The subject is 'The water' (singular), so 'is', not agreeing with 'bottles'.

questions.stem: The news about the school trip ____ exciting.

explain.why: 'news' looks plural but is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.
'be' is not a finite verb and does not agree with 'The news'; 'is' is needed.
'news' is treated as singular, so 'were' is wrong.

solution: The news about the school trip is exciting.
'news' is singular, so 'is'.

questions.stem: Neither Ali nor his friends ____ finished the project.

explain.why: 'was' cannot be followed by 'finished' to form a perfect tense.
'were' cannot be followed by 'finished' to form the perfect tense; 'have finished' is needed.
With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'his friends', which is plural.

solution: Neither Ali nor his friends have finished the project.
'neither ... nor' follows the nearer subject: 'his friends' is plural, so 'have'.

questions.stem: Each of the P6 pupils ____ a copy of the revision notes.

explain.why: 'Each' is singular, even though 'pupils' comes right before the blank.
'are' does not suit 'a copy of the notes' and does not agree with 'Each'.
'do' is an auxiliary and cannot mean 'possess' here.

solution: Each of the P6 pupils has a copy of the revision notes.
'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb: has.

questions.stem: A number of pupils ____ absent today because of the flu.

explain.why: 'was' is singular, but 'a number of pupils' is plural; the time 'today' also needs present.
'has been' is singular; 'a number of pupils' is plural.
'A number of' means 'several', so the verb is plural.

solution: A number of pupils are absent today because of the flu.
'A number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb: are.

questions.stem: The number of pupils in the choir ____ increased this year.

explain.why: 'The number of' is singular, so it takes 'has', not 'have'.
'were' cannot be followed by 'increased' to form a perfect tense.
'are' cannot be followed by 'increased' to form a perfect tense.

solution: The number of pupils in the choir has increased this year.
'The number of' is singular, so 'has increased'.

questions.stem: The police ____ questioning two men outside the shopping centre.

explain.why: 'police' is always plural, so 'is' is wrong.
'has been' is singular; 'the police' is plural.
'police' takes a plural verb, and 'was' is singular.

solution: The police are questioning two men outside the shopping centre.
'The police' is plural, so 'are'.

questions.stem: The quality of the cookies sold at the school fair ____ improved a great deal.

explain.why: 'were' cannot be followed by 'improved' to form the perfect tense.
'have' agrees with the nearby 'cookies', but the subject is 'The quality', which is singular.
'are' cannot be followed by 'improved' to form the perfect tense.

solution: The quality of the cookies sold at the school fair has improved a great deal.
The subject is 'The quality' (singular), so 'has improved'.

questions.stem: The list of items to bring for the camp ____ pinned on the notice board for a week, so check it before you pack.

explain.why: 'have been' agrees with the nearby 'items', but the subject is 'The list', which is singular.
'are' agrees with the nearby 'items', and 'for a week' needs a perfect tense.
'were' is plural, but the subject is 'The list' (singular).

solution: The list of items to bring for the camp has been pinned on the notice board for a week, so check it before you pack.
The subject is 'The list' (singular), so 'has been pinned'.

questions.stem: Not only the pupils but also their form teacher ____ excited about the camp for weeks.

explain.why: 'were' is plural, and 'for weeks' needs a perfect tense.
With 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'their form teacher', which is singular.
'are' is plural, and 'for weeks' needs a perfect tense.

solution: Not only the pupils but also their form teacher has been excited about the camp for weeks.
'not only ... but also' agrees with the nearer subject (singular): has been.

questions.stem: The teacher, together with her P6 pupils, ____ at the MRT station since 7 a.m.

explain.why: 'since 7 a.m.' needs a perfect tense, not past continuous.
'together with her P6 pupils' does not make the subject plural; the subject is only 'The teacher'.
'since 7 a.m.' needs a perfect tense, not simple present continuous.

solution: The teacher, together with her P6 pupils, has been waiting at the MRT station since 7 a.m.
'together with' does not change the subject; 'since' needs the perfect: has been waiting.

questions.stem: There is ____ juice left in the jug.

explain.why: 'many' is used with countable plural nouns, not with uncountable 'juice'.
'a number of' goes with plural countable nouns, but 'juice' is uncountable.
'a few' is used with countable nouns, but 'juice' is uncountable.

solution: There is a little juice left in the jug.
'juice' is uncountable, so 'a little'.

questions.stem: How ____ pupils are there in your class?

explain.why: 'a little' goes with uncountable nouns, not 'pupils'.
'much' is for uncountable nouns, but 'pupils' is countable.
'little' goes with uncountable nouns, not 'pupils'.

solution: How many pupils are there in your class?
'pupils' is countable, so 'How many'.

questions.stem: Could I have ____ apple from the basket, please?

explain.why: 'few' needs a plural noun, but 'apple' is singular.
'many' needs a plural noun, but 'apple' is singular.
'apple' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an', not 'a'.

solution: Could I have an apple from the basket, please?
Before a vowel sound, use 'an': an apple.

questions.stem: She drank ____ water after the run.

explain.why: 'many' is used with countable plural nouns, not uncountable 'water'.
'a' is used before a singular countable noun, but 'water' is uncountable.
'few' is used with countable plural nouns, not uncountable 'water'.

solution: She drank some water after the run.
'water' is uncountable, so 'some'.

questions.stem: We have ____ time left, so we must hurry.

explain.why: 'few' goes with countable nouns, but 'time' here is uncountable.
'a few' goes with countable nouns, but 'time' here is uncountable.
'several' goes with plural countable nouns, but 'time' here is uncountable.

solution: We have little time left, so we must hurry.
'time' is uncountable and the meaning is 'not enough', so 'little'.

questions.stem: There were so ____ people at the hawker centre that we had to wait for a table.

explain.why: 'little' is for uncountable nouns, and it would mean there were hardly any people.
'much' is for uncountable nouns, but 'people' is a countable plural.
'so few' would mean there were hardly any people, which does not explain the wait.

solution: There were so many people at the hawker centre that we had to wait for a table.
'people' is countable and the meaning is 'a large number', so 'so many'.

questions.stem: He has ____ friends, so he often feels lonely.

explain.why: 'a few' means some, which is positive; 'feels lonely' needs the negative 'few'.
'any' is used mainly in negatives and questions, not in a positive statement like this.
'a little' goes with uncountable nouns, but 'friends' is countable.

solution: He has few friends, so he often feels lonely.
'friends' is countable and the meaning is 'hardly any', so 'few'.

questions.stem: We have ____ sugar left, so we can still bake a small cake.

explain.why: 'a number of' goes with plural countable nouns, but 'sugar' is uncountable.
'a few' goes with countable nouns, but 'sugar' is uncountable.
'few' goes with countable nouns, but 'sugar' is uncountable.

solution: We have a little sugar left, so we can still bake a small cake.
'sugar' is uncountable and 'can still bake' is positive, so 'a little'.

questions.stem: ____ pupil in the class must hand in the form by Friday.

explain.why: 'Several' needs a plural noun, but 'pupil' is singular.
'All' needs a plural noun, but 'pupil' is singular.
'Many' needs a plural noun, but 'pupil' is singular.

solution: Every pupil in the class must hand in the form by Friday.
'pupil' is singular, so 'Every'.

questions.stem: The more homework Kiara had, ____ time she had to play.

explain.why: 'the least' is a superlative, but the sentence compares two changes.
'fewer' is used with countable nouns, but 'time' is uncountable.
'The more ..., the less ...' needs 'the' before the second comparative.

solution: The more homework Kiara had, the less time she had to play.
'time' is uncountable, so 'the less' in 'the more ..., the less ...'.

questions.stem: Hardly ____ pupils came to the extra class because of the rain, so it was cancelled.

explain.why: 'a little' goes with uncountable nouns, but 'pupils' is countable.
'hardly a few' is not used; 'hardly' goes with 'any'.
'hardly' is already negative, so adding 'no' makes a double negative.

solution: Hardly any pupils came to the extra class because of the rain, so it was cancelled.
'hardly' is followed by 'any': Hardly any pupils came.

questions.stem: Not all the answers were correct; ____ were wrong.

explain.why: 'any' is used mainly in negatives and questions, but this is a positive statement.
'no' would say none were wrong, which contradicts 'Not all'.
'every' needs a singular noun, and 'every were' is ungrammatical.

solution: Not all the answers were correct; some were wrong.
'Not all were correct' means some were wrong, so 'some'.

questions.stem: We spent so ____ money on the gift that we had none left for the card.

explain.why: 'too' would need 'to' after it, not 'that'.
'many' is used with countable nouns, but 'money' is uncountable.
'so such money' is ungrammatical; 'such' cannot follow 'so'.

solution: We spent so much money on the gift that we had none left for the card.
'money' is uncountable, so 'so much ... that ...'.

questions.stem: You like chicken rice, ____?

explain.why: 'like' uses 'do', so the tag needs 'don't', not 'aren't'.
The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.
The sentence is in the present, so the tag needs 'don't', not past 'didn't'.

solution: You like chicken rice, don't you?
Positive present statement with 'like': the tag is 'don't you'.

questions.stem: Ben can swim, ____?

explain.why: The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.
The statement has the modal 'can', so the tag needs 'can't', not 'isn't'.
The statement uses 'can', so the tag repeats 'can', not 'does'.

solution: Ben can swim, can't he?
The tag repeats the modal 'can' in the opposite polarity: can't he.

questions.stem: The pupils aren't late, ____?

explain.why: 'The pupils' is plural, so the pronoun must be 'they', not 'it'.
The statement is negative, so the tag must be positive.
The statement uses 'are', so the tag repeats 'are', not 'do'.

solution: The pupils aren't late, are they?
Negative statement with 'are': the tag is positive 'are they'.

questions.stem: Let's go to the library after school, ____?

explain.why: After 'Let's' the tag is 'shall we', not a negative 'don't we'.
After 'Let's', the tag is 'shall we'.
'let us' is not a question tag.

solution: Let's go to the library after school, shall we?
'Let's ...' takes the tag 'shall we?'.

questions.stem: She didn't finish her homework, ____?

explain.why: The statement uses 'didn't', so the tag repeats 'did', not 'is'.
The statement is past, so the tag must use 'did', not 'does'.
The statement has 'didn't', so the tag uses 'did', not 'had'.

solution: She didn't finish her homework, did she?
Negative past statement: the tag is positive 'did she'.

questions.stem: Everyone is ready for the performance, ____?

explain.why: The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.
The statement uses 'is', so the tag repeats 'be' as 'aren't', not 'don't'.
The statement is present ('is'), so the tag cannot be past 'weren't'.

solution: Everyone is ready for the performance, aren't they?
'Everyone' takes 'they' in the tag; positive statement gives negative 'aren't they'.

questions.stem: I am the tallest in the class, ____?

explain.why: The statement uses 'am', so the tag uses 'be', not 'have'.
The statement uses 'am', so the tag uses 'be', not 'do'.
The subject is 'I', so the tag pronoun must be 'I', not 'it'.

solution: I am the tallest in the class, aren't I?
After 'I am', the standard tag is 'aren't I'.

questions.stem: Nothing was wrong with the lift, ____?

explain.why: 'Nothing' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.
'Nothing' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive, and the pronoun should be 'it'.
The statement is past ('was'), so the tag needs 'was', not 'is'.

solution: Nothing was wrong with the lift, was it?
'Nothing' is a negative word, so the tag is positive: was it.

questions.stem: There is a queue outside the shop, ____?

explain.why: After 'There is', the tag repeats 'there', not 'it'.
'There is' is singular, so the tag uses 'isn't', not 'aren't'.
The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.

solution: There is a queue outside the shop, isn't there?
'There is ...' takes the tag 'isn't there'.

questions.stem: Your parents have never been to Sentosa, ____?

explain.why: The statement is present perfect, so the tag needs 'have', not 'had'.
The statement uses 'have', so the tag repeats 'have', not 'did'.
'never' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.

solution: Your parents have never been to Sentosa, have they?
'never' is negative, so the tag is positive: have they.

questions.stem: She used to take the school bus, ____?

explain.why: 'used to take' has no 'was', so 'wasn't' does not fit.
'used to' takes the past 'did' in the tag, not 'usedn't'.
'used to' is past, so the tag needs 'didn't', not 'doesn't'.

solution: She used to take the school bus, didn't she?
'used to' takes 'didn't' in the tag.

questions.stem: You wouldn't mind waiting outside, ____?

explain.why: The statement is negative, so the tag must be positive.
The statement has 'would', so the tag repeats 'would', not 'will'.
The statement has the modal 'would', so the tag repeats 'would'.

solution: You wouldn't mind waiting outside, would you?
The tag repeats 'would' in the opposite polarity: would you.

questions.stem: Hardly anyone came to the meeting, ____?

explain.why: 'Hardly' is negative, so the tag must be positive, and 'anyone' takes 'they'.
'anyone' is referred to with 'they' in a tag, not 'he'.
'Hardly' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.

solution: Hardly anyone came to the meeting, did they?
'Hardly' is a negative word, so the tag is positive: did they.

questions.stem: Neither of them wanted to join the CCA, ____?

explain.why: 'Neither' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.
The statement is past ('wanted'), so the tag needs 'did', not 'do'.
'Neither of them' refers to people, so the tag pronoun is 'they', not 'it'.

solution: Neither of them wanted to join the CCA, did they?
'Neither' is negative, so the tag is positive: did they.

questions.stem: We stayed indoors ____ it was raining heavily.

explain.why: 'so' introduces a result, but 'it was raining' is the cause.
'although' shows contrast, but the rain is the reason.
'unless' means 'if not', which does not fit a past reason.

solution: We stayed indoors because it was raining heavily.
The rain is the reason, so use 'because'.

questions.stem: I wanted to buy the toy, ____ I did not have enough money.

explain.why: 'because' would say that wanting the toy was caused by having no money.
'so' shows result, but not having money is a contrast to wanting.
'or' shows a choice, not a contrast.

solution: I wanted to buy the toy, but I did not have enough money.
Contrast between wanting and being unable: 'but'.

questions.stem: Please wash your hands ____ you eat.

explain.why: 'so' shows result and cannot join the two actions this way.
'unless' means 'if not', which does not fit the sequence of washing and eating.
'although' shows contrast, but this is a sequence.

solution: Please wash your hands before you eat.
Washing comes first, then eating: 'before'.

questions.stem: Hurry up, ____ you will miss the bus.

explain.why: 'but' shows contrast, not a warning of a result.
'so' would say that missing the bus is the aim of hurrying.
'and' would say that hurrying causes missing the bus.

solution: Hurry up, or you will miss the bus.
A command followed by a warning: 'or'.

questions.stem: You cannot enter the lab ____ you wear safety goggles.

explain.why: 'though' shows contrast, not a condition.
'as' gives a reason and does not state a condition.
'if' would say you cannot enter when you wear goggles, which is the opposite.

solution: You cannot enter the lab unless you wear safety goggles.
'unless' means 'if you do not': cannot enter unless you wear goggles.

questions.stem: He worked hard; ____, he did not pass the test.

explain.why: 'moreover' adds a similar point, not a contrast.
'therefore' shows result, but failing is the opposite of what was expected.
'besides' adds a point and does not show contrast.

solution: He worked hard; however, he did not pass the test.
A contrast between two sentences needs 'however'.

questions.stem: Not only did she win the race, ____ she also broke the school record.

explain.why: 'Not only' pairs with 'but', not 'or'.
'Not only' pairs with 'but', not 'and'.
'Not only' pairs with 'but', not 'so'.

solution: Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the school record.
'not only ... but also ...' is a fixed pair.

questions.stem: I will wait here ____ you come back.

explain.why: 'because' gives a reason, but the sentence gives a time limit.
'since' looks back to a past starting point, but this is about the future.
'unless' means 'if not', which does not fit waiting up to a time.

solution: I will wait here until you come back.
Waiting up to a time takes 'until'.

questions.stem: ____ the heavy rain, the match was not cancelled.

explain.why: 'Because' would give a reason for not cancelling, which is the wrong logic.
'Although' must be followed by a clause, but 'the heavy rain' is a noun phrase.
'However' links separate sentences and cannot start a phrase like this.

solution: Despite the heavy rain, the match was not cancelled.
'Despite' + noun phrase shows contrast.

questions.stem: The school fair was a success ____ the poor weather.

explain.why: 'because of' would say the weather caused the success.
'even though' must be followed by a clause, not a noun phrase.
'although' must be followed by a clause, not a noun phrase.

solution: The school fair was a success in spite of the poor weather.
'in spite of' + noun phrase shows contrast.

questions.stem: He studied hard ____ that he could pass the test.

explain.why: 'very that' is not a correct pattern.
'such that' is a different pattern and does not express purpose here.
'as that' is not a pattern for purpose; 'so that' is needed.

solution: He studied hard so that he could pass the test.
'so that' expresses purpose.

questions.stem: Rina ran so fast ____ she overtook all the other runners.

explain.why: 'so fast as' is used for comparison, not a result.
'than' is used with comparatives, not with 'so ... '.
'so fast ____' needs 'that' to show the result, not 'which'.

solution: Rina ran so fast that she overtook all the other runners.
'so + adjective/adverb + that + result'.

questions.stem: The girl ____ sits beside me is my cousin.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession and needs a noun after it, but here it is followed by the verb 'sits'.
'why' asks for a reason and cannot refer back to 'The girl'.
'which' is for things, but 'The girl' is a person.

solution: The girl who sits beside me is my cousin.
For a person as subject, use 'who'.

questions.stem: This is the book ____ I borrowed from the library.

explain.why: 'who' is for people, but 'book' is a thing.
'whose' shows possession, but the clause is about the thing that was borrowed.
'where' is used for places, but 'book' is not a place.

solution: This is the book that I borrowed from the library.
For a thing as object, use 'that' (or 'which').

questions.stem: That is the boy ____ bicycle was stolen.

explain.why: 'whom' cannot show possession.
'which' is for things, but 'the boy' is a person.
'who' cannot be followed directly by the noun 'bicycle'; possession needs 'whose'.

solution: That is the boy whose bicycle was stolen.
Possession by a person: 'whose bicycle'.

questions.stem: The hawker centre ____ we have lunch every Friday is very crowded.

explain.why: 'who' is for people, but 'hawker centre' is a place.
'whose' shows possession, but the clause tells where we have lunch.
'which' would need a preposition, as in 'at which', to show the place.

solution: The hawker centre where we have lunch every Friday is very crowded.
A place where an action happens takes 'where'.

questions.stem: I do not know ____ left the lights on.

explain.why: 'whom' is for the object, but here the unknown person is the subject of 'left'.
'why' asks for a reason, but 'left' needs a subject that tells who left.
'whose' needs a noun after it to show ownership.

solution: I do not know who left the lights on.
The missing person is the subject of 'left', so 'who'.

questions.stem: Mrs Lee, ____ taught me in Primary 4, retired last year.

explain.why: 'whose' needs a noun after it, but 'taught' follows.
'whom' is for the object, but Mrs Lee is the subject of 'taught'.
'she' repeats the subject instead of joining the clauses; a relative pronoun is needed.

solution: Mrs Lee, who taught me in Primary 4, retired last year.
Extra information about a named person, subject of the clause: 'who'.

questions.stem: The pupil to ____ I lent my pencil case forgot to return it.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession, but the clause is about who received the pencil case.
After a preposition ('to'), 'whom' is used, not 'who'.
'which' is for things, but 'The pupil' is a person.

solution: The pupil to whom I lent my pencil case forgot to return it.
After a preposition, use 'whom' for a person.

questions.stem: She told us about the trip, ____ we found very interesting.

explain.why: 'what' cannot add information about the trip after a comma.
'whose' shows possession and needs a noun after it, but the clause is not about owning.
'that' is not used after a comma to add extra information.

solution: She told us about the trip, which we found very interesting.
After a comma, extra information about a thing takes 'which'.

questions.stem: He asked me ____ I would like to join the chess club.

explain.why: 'what' would need to be the object of 'join', but 'to join the chess club' already has its object.
'asked me that' does not introduce a yes/no question.
'whatever' does not introduce a yes/no reported question.

solution: He asked me whether I would like to join the chess club.
A yes/no reported question uses 'whether' (or 'if').

questions.stem: Everything ____ the guide told us about the old temple was fascinating.

explain.why: 'who' is for people, but 'Everything' is not a person.
'whose' shows possession, but the clause is not about owning.
'what' cannot follow 'Everything'; after 'everything' use 'that'.

solution: Everything that the guide told us about the old temple was fascinating.
After 'everything', the relative pronoun is 'that'.

questions.stem: Ali hurt ____ while playing basketball.

explain.why: The subject and object are the same person, so the reflexive 'himself' is needed.
'Ali' is one person, so 'themselves' does not agree.
'his' is a possessive and needs a noun after it.

solution: Ali hurt himself while playing basketball.
When the object is the same person as the subject, use the reflexive: himself.

questions.stem: Ali and Ben forgot ____ lunch boxes at home.

explain.why: 'theirs' stands alone and cannot come before a noun.
'they' is a subject pronoun and cannot come before a noun to show ownership.
'them' is an object pronoun and cannot come before a noun to show ownership.

solution: Ali and Ben forgot their lunch boxes at home.
A possessive determiner before a noun: their lunch boxes.

questions.stem: That pencil case is not mine; it belongs to Siti. It is ____.

explain.why: 'her' must be followed by a noun; without one, use 'hers'.
'she' is a subject pronoun, but the blank needs a possessive.
'herself' means she did something to herself, not ownership.

solution: That pencil case is not mine; it belongs to Siti. It is hers.
A possessive pronoun that stands alone: hers.

questions.stem: Between you and ____, I think the quiz will be difficult.

explain.why: 'myself' is used only when 'I' is the subject of the same clause.
'mine' is a possessive pronoun, not an object after 'between'.
After the preposition 'between', an object pronoun 'me' is needed, not 'I'.

solution: Between you and me, I think the quiz will be difficult.
A pronoun after a preposition takes the object form: between you and me.

questions.stem: The teacher asked the pupils to do the task by ____, without any help.

explain.why: 'theirs' is a possessive pronoun and does not mean 'alone'.
'their' is a possessive determiner and needs a noun after it.
'their own selves' is not the standard phrase; the idiom is 'by themselves'.

solution: The teacher asked the pupils to do the task by themselves, without any help.
'by + reflexive' means alone: by themselves.

questions.stem: The puppy kept chasing ____ tail round the garden.

explain.why: The puppy is one animal, so 'their' does not agree.
'it's' means 'it is' or 'it has'; the possessive is 'its'.
'it' cannot come before a noun to show ownership; the possessive form is needed.

solution: The puppy kept chasing its tail round the garden.
The possessive of 'it' has no apostrophe: its tail.

questions.stem: Nobody except Tom and ____ knew about the surprise.

explain.why: 'except' is a preposition, so the object pronoun 'me' is needed, not 'I'.
'mine' is a possessive pronoun, not an object after 'except'.
'myself' cannot be used when there is no 'I' as the subject of the clause.

solution: Nobody except Tom and me knew about the surprise.
After 'except', use the object form: Tom and me.

questions.stem: The principal praised Kai Xin and ____ for helping to organise the fair.

explain.why: 'mine' is a possessive pronoun and cannot be the object of 'praised'.
'I' is a subject pronoun, but here the pronoun is the object of 'praised'.
'myself' is used when the subject is 'I', but the subject here is 'The principal'.

solution: The principal praised Kai Xin and me for helping to organise the fair.
The object of 'praised' takes the object form: Kai Xin and me.

questions.stem: You ____ wear your school badge every day.

explain.why: 'could' shows ability or possibility, not an obligation.
'may' gives permission or shows a possibility, but a school rule needs 'must'.
'might' shows a weak possibility, not a rule.

solution: You must wear your school badge every day.
A rule or duty uses 'must'.

questions.stem: ____ I borrow your eraser, please?

explain.why: 'Shall I borrow' does not ask permission to take something.
'Would I borrow' asks about a possible situation, not permission.
'Do I borrow' asks about a habit, not permission.

solution: May I borrow your eraser, please?
Asking permission politely uses 'May I'.

questions.stem: You ____ run along the corridor; it is dangerous.

explain.why: 'wouldn't' shows an unwillingness or a hypothetical, not a prohibition.
'needn't' means 'it is not necessary', but running is forbidden.
'couldn't' shows past inability or doubt, not a rule.

solution: You mustn't run along the corridor; it is dangerous.
A prohibition uses 'mustn't'.

questions.stem: You ____ bring an umbrella; the forecast says it will be sunny all day.

explain.why: 'wouldn't bring' does not say there is no need.
'mustn't' would forbid bringing an umbrella, but it is only unnecessary.
'couldn't' shows inability, not lack of need.

solution: You needn't bring an umbrella; the forecast says it will be sunny all day.
No need to do something uses 'needn't'.

questions.stem: When I was young, I ____ swim, but now I swim like a fish.

explain.why: 'can't' is present, but 'when I was young' needs the past.
'needn't' means 'no need to', not inability.
'shouldn't' gives advice and does not describe a past inability.

solution: When I was young, I couldn't swim, but now I swim like a fish.
Past inability uses 'couldn't'.

questions.stem: If you had told me earlier, I ____ have helped you.

explain.why: 'shall have helped' is not used in an unreal past condition.
'can have helped' does not fit a past unreal condition.
'will have' does not fit a past unreal condition.

solution: If you had told me earlier, I would have helped you.
A past unreal condition ('had told') takes 'would have' in the result.

questions.stem: If it rains tomorrow, we ____ the picnic.

explain.why: 'had cancelled' is past perfect and does not fit a future situation.
The simple past 'cancelled' does not fit a future real possibility.
'would cancel' belongs to an unlikely situation, but a rainy day tomorrow is a real possibility.

solution: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
Real possibility: 'If' + present, 'will' + verb.

questions.stem: If I were you, I ____ the teacher for help.

explain.why: 'If I were you' is an imaginary situation, so 'would' is needed, not 'will'.
'had asked' is past perfect and does not fit this present imaginary situation.
The result of an imaginary condition needs 'would', not the simple past.

solution: If I were you, I would ask the teacher for help.
Imaginary present condition: 'If I were', 'would' + verb.

questions.stem: If the bus had come earlier, we ____ late for the show.

explain.why: 'would not have being' is wrong; the participle needed is 'been'.
The result clause needs 'would not have been', not past perfect.
'will not be' is a future form and does not fit a condition about the past.

solution: If the bus had come earlier, we would not have been late for the show.
Past unreal condition: 'If' + past perfect, 'would have' + participle.

questions.stem: Unless you ____ faster, you will miss the bus.

explain.why: 'unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'not' makes a double negative.
After 'unless', the verb stays in the present, not 'will'.
A real future condition needs the simple present, not the simple past.

solution: Unless you run faster, you will miss the bus.
'Unless' + simple present (positive form): Unless you run faster ...

questions.stem: I would not have been scolded if I ____ my homework.

explain.why: 'would do' belongs in the result clause, not after 'if'.
A past unreal condition needs past perfect, not the simple past.
'have done' does not fit a condition about the past.

solution: I would not have been scolded if I had done my homework.
Past unreal condition: 'if' + past perfect: had done.

questions.stem: Hui Min ate her noodles ____ at the hawker centre.

explain.why: 'slowness' is a noun, which cannot describe the verb 'ate'
'slowest' is a superlative adjective, so it cannot describe how she ate
'slow' is an adjective, but an adverb is needed to describe how she ate

solution: Hui Min ate her noodles slowly at the hawker centre.
'slowly' is an adverb because it tells how Hui Min ate.

questions.stem: The bus ____ outside our school every morning.

explain.why: 'bus' is singular, so the verb needs -s: 'stop' does not agree
'stopping' alone is not a finished verb for this sentence
'to stop' is an infinitive and cannot be the main verb

solution: The bus stops outside our school every morning.
'stops' is the verb: it tells what the bus does, and it agrees with the singular 'bus'.

questions.stem: The ____ canteen opened at seven.

explain.why: 'noisily' is an adverb, but a word describing the noun 'canteen' is needed
'noise' is a noun, so it cannot describe 'canteen'
'noises' is a plural noun, so it cannot describe 'canteen'

solution: The noisy canteen opened at seven.
'noisy' is an adjective because it describes the noun 'canteen'.

questions.stem: Ravi found a seat, and ____ sat down quietly.

explain.why: 'his' is a possessive and cannot be the subject of 'sat'
'himself' is a reflexive pronoun and cannot be the subject
'him' is an object pronoun, but the subject of 'sat' needs a subject pronoun

solution: Ravi found a seat, and he sat down quietly.
'he' is a pronoun that takes the place of 'Ravi' as the subject.

questions.stem: Anna put her bag ____ the chair.

explain.why: 'so' is a conjunction and cannot link 'bag' to 'chair'
'very' is an adverb and cannot link 'bag' to 'chair'
'but' is a conjunction and cannot show where the bag was put

solution: Anna put her bag on the chair.
'on' is a preposition because it shows the position of the bag in relation to the chair.

questions.stem: I wanted to play outside, ____ it started to rain and I had to stay in.

explain.why: 'quickly' is an adverb and cannot join two clauses
'because' gives a reason, but the rain stopped her playing; it is not why she wanted to play
'under' is a preposition and cannot join two clauses

solution: I wanted to play outside, but it started to rain and I had to stay in.
'but' is a conjunction because it joins two clauses and shows contrast.

questions.stem: ____ is a country that Dev's family loves to visit.

explain.why: a proper noun names one particular country, so 'a' is wrong
a proper noun like 'Japan' does not take 'the'
a proper noun names one particular country, so 'an' is wrong

solution: Japan is a country that Dev's family loves to visit.
'Japan' is a proper noun: it names a particular place, so it takes no article.

questions.stem: Mum quickly cooked ____ for us.

explain.why: 'dine' is a verb, but a noun is needed as the thing cooked
'hungry' is an adjective, not the thing that was cooked
'dined' is a verb, but a noun is needed as the thing cooked

solution: Mum quickly cooked dinner for us.
'dinner' is a noun because it names the thing Mum cooked.

questions.stem: Grandma ____ early on weekdays.

explain.why: 'sleepy' is an adjective, not a verb
'Grandma' is singular, so 'sleep' does not agree
'sleeping' alone is not a finished verb here

solution: Grandma sleeps early on weekdays.
'sleeps' is the verb because it tells what Grandma does.

questions.stem: Ben carried a ____ bag up the stairs.

explain.why: 'heaviness' is a noun and cannot describe 'bag'
'heavily' is an adverb, but a word describing the noun 'bag' is needed
'heave' is a verb and cannot describe 'bag'

solution: Ben carried a heavy bag up the stairs.
'heavy' is an adjective because it describes the noun 'bag'.

questions.stem: The baby slept ____.

explain.why: 'soundness' is a noun, but an adverb is needed to describe how the baby slept
'unsound' is an adjective, so it cannot describe how the baby slept
'sounding' is a verb form, not a word telling how the baby slept

solution: The baby slept soundly.
'soundly' is an adverb because it tells how the baby slept.

questions.stem: We will visit the zoo ____.

explain.why: an adverb of time like 'tomorrow' takes no 'the'
an adverb of time like 'tomorrow' takes no preposition
an adverb of time like 'tomorrow' takes no preposition

solution: We will visit the zoo tomorrow.
'tomorrow' is an adverb of time: it tells when, and needs no extra word.

questions.stem: Please give the book to ____.

explain.why: 'mine' is a possessive pronoun meaning 'belonging to me'; it does not name the person receiving the book
'my' is a possessive and must be followed by a noun
'I' is a subject pronoun, but 'to' needs an object pronoun

solution: Please give the book to me.
'me' is an object pronoun used after the preposition 'to'.

questions.stem: The ball rolled ____ the bench.

explain.why: 'slowly' is an adverb and cannot link 'rolled' to 'the bench'
'roll' is a verb and cannot link to 'the bench'
'and' is a conjunction and cannot show where the ball went

solution: The ball rolled under the bench.
'under' is a preposition because it shows where the ball rolled in relation to the bench.

questions.stem: Jun Wei stayed home ____ he was ill.

explain.why: 'beside' is a preposition and cannot join two clauses
'quickly' is an adverb and cannot join two clauses
'him' is a pronoun and cannot join two clauses

solution: Jun Wei stayed home because he was ill.
'because' is a conjunction: it joins two clauses and gives a reason.

questions.stem: Siti and ____ kicked the ball into the net.

explain.why: 'me' is an object pronoun, but a subject is needed before 'kicked'
'myself' is reflexive and cannot be a subject
'mine' is a possessive pronoun and cannot be a subject

solution: Siti and I kicked the ball into the net.
'I' is the subject pronoun: the subject is the one doing the action.

questions.stem: The new librarian ____ smiling at the pupils.

explain.why: 'were' is a plural past form, so it does not agree with the singular 'librarian'
'librarian' is singular, so 'are' does not agree
'be' is the base form and cannot be the verb after the singular subject 'The new librarian' here

solution: The new librarian is smiling at the pupils.
The subject 'The new librarian' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.

questions.stem: The girl bought a drink and gave ____ to her brother.

explain.why: 'they' is a subject pronoun and cannot be the object of 'gave'
'she' is a subject pronoun and cannot be the object of 'gave'
'I' is a subject pronoun and cannot be the object of 'gave'

solution: The girl bought a drink and gave it to her brother.
'it' is an object pronoun standing for 'a drink'.

questions.stem: The bicycle is broken, so Dad is repairing ____ carefully.

explain.why: 'they' is plural, but 'the bicycle' is singular
'its' is a possessive and must be followed by a noun
'itself' is reflexive and must refer back to the subject 'Dad', but Dad is not 'it'

solution: The bicycle is broken, so Dad is repairing it carefully.
'it' is the object pronoun for 'the bicycle'.

questions.stem: Mum packed three ____ of books.

explain.why: 'box's' shows ownership, not a plural
'box' does not change -x to -ies
nouns ending in -x add -es, not -s

solution: Mum packed three boxes of books.
'boxes' is the plural noun: nouns ending in -x add -es.

questions.stem: Several ____ played in the park.

explain.why: 'children' is already plural, so no extra -s
'child' is singular, but 'Several' needs a plural noun
'child' has an irregular plural

solution: Several children played in the park.
'children' is the irregular plural noun of 'child'.

questions.stem: Two cats ____ sleeping on the sofa.

explain.why: 'was' is singular, but the subject is plural
'Two cats' is plural, so 'is' does not agree
'am' is used only with 'I'

solution: Two cats are sleeping on the sofa.
'Two cats' is a plural subject, so the verb is 'are'.

questions.stem: We ____ the classroom after school yesterday.

explain.why: 'are cleaning' is present continuous, but 'yesterday' is past
'clean' is present, but 'yesterday' is past
'will clean' is future, but 'yesterday' is past

solution: We cleaned the classroom after school yesterday.
'cleaned' is the simple past tense because 'yesterday' is already over.

questions.stem: Our class ____ the museum next week.

explain.why: 'visited' is past, but 'next week' is future
'visiting' alone is not a finished verb for this sentence
'has visited' is present perfect, but 'next week' is future

solution: Our class will visit the museum next week.
'will visit' is the future tense because 'next week' has not come yet.

questions.stem: The sun ____ in the east and sets in the west.

explain.why: 'rose' is past, but 'sets' is present and this is a fact that is always true
'was rising' is past continuous, but 'sets' is present and the fact is always true
'will rise' is future, but 'sets' is present and the fact is true all the time

solution: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
'rises' is the simple present tense, used for facts that are always true, matching 'sets'.

questions.stem: Ali is ____ than his brother.

explain.why: short adjectives add -er, not 'more'
'tallish' means somewhat tall and does not compare with 'than'
'tallest' compares three or more, but only two are compared here

solution: Ali is taller than his brother.
'taller' is the comparative adjective: it compares two people.

questions.stem: Of all the singers, Mei sang the ____.

explain.why: 'good' and 'well' have an irregular superlative, 'best', not 'most good'
'good' and 'well' have an irregular superlative, 'best', not 'goodest'
'better' compares two, but 'of all the singers' needs the superlative

solution: Of all the singers, Mei sang the best.
'best' is the irregular superlative of 'good' and 'well': it compares Mei with all the other singers.

questions.stem: The ____ firefighter rescued the kitten.

explain.why: 'bravely' is an adverb, but a word describing the noun 'firefighter' is needed
'bravery' is a noun, so it cannot describe 'firefighter'
'braves' is a noun or verb form, not a describing word

solution: The brave firefighter rescued the kitten.
'brave' is an adjective because it describes the noun 'firefighter'.

questions.stem: Mei Ling walked ____ after school.

explain.why: 'in home' is not correct English here
'the home' makes home a noun, which would need 'to' before it to show direction
'home' used as an adverb takes no preposition

solution: Mei Ling walked home after school.
'home' is an adverb here, telling where she walked, so it takes no 'to'.

questions.stem: Ben is a ____ swimmer.

explain.why: 'fastness' is a noun, so it cannot describe 'swimmer'
'fast' is both adjective and adverb; 'fastly' is not a word
'quickly' is an adverb, so it cannot describe a noun

solution: Ben is a fast swimmer.
'fast' is an adjective here because it describes the noun 'swimmer'.

questions.stem: Mei sings ____ in the school choir.

explain.why: 'nicer' is a comparative adjective, not an adverb
'goodly' is not the adverb of 'good'
'good' is an adjective, but an adverb is needed to describe 'sings'

solution: Mei sings well in the school choir.
'well' is the adverb of 'good': it tells how Mei sings.

questions.stem: The team trained ____ for the finals.

explain.why: 'hardness' is a noun, so it cannot describe 'trained'
'hardly' means almost not, which changes the meaning
'hards' is not a word

solution: The team trained hard for the finals.
'hard' is an adverb here, telling how they trained; 'hardly' means 'almost not'.

questions.stem: The bus arrived ____ this morning.

explain.why: 'lateness' is a noun, so it cannot describe 'arrived'
'latest' is a superlative adjective, so it cannot describe 'arrived'
'lately' means recently, not behind time

solution: The bus arrived late this morning.
'late' is an adverb telling when or how the bus arrived; 'lately' means recently.

questions.stem: The boy ____ sits beside me is called Ravi.

explain.why: 'whom' is an object form, but here the word is the subject of 'sits'
'which' refers to things, but 'boy' is a person
'whose' shows ownership and needs a noun after it

solution: The boy who sits beside me is called Ravi.
'who' is a relative pronoun referring to a person and acting as subject.

questions.stem: Sam has ____ to his pen pal.

explain.why: 'writing' is a present participle and does not fit after 'has'
'wrote' is simple past; after 'has' the past participle is needed
'writes' is simple present and does not fit after 'has'

solution: Sam has written to his pen pal.
'written' is the past participle of 'write', used after 'has'.

questions.stem: The children have ____ all the cake.

explain.why: 'eating' is a present participle, but 'have' needs the past participle
'eat' is irregular, so 'eated' is not a word
'ate' is simple past; after 'have' the past participle is needed

solution: The children have eaten all the cake.
'eaten' is the past participle of 'eat', used after 'have'.

questions.stem: When we arrived, the guests had already ____.

explain.why: 'going' is a present participle, but 'had' needs the past participle
'went' is simple past; after 'had' the past participle is needed
'go' is irregular, so 'goed' is not a word

solution: When we arrived, the guests had already gone.
'gone' is the past participle of 'go', used after 'had'.

questions.stem: Yesterday, Lina ____ twenty laps.

explain.why: 'swim' is irregular, so 'swimmed' is not a word
'swimming' needs 'was' before it and does not fit 'Yesterday'
'swum' is the past participle and needs 'has' or 'had' before it

solution: Yesterday, Lina swam twenty laps.
'swam' is the simple past tense of 'swim'.

questions.stem: Rina ____ already finished her homework, so she can play now.

explain.why: 'is' cannot form the present perfect: 'is already finished' is not correct grammar, 'has' is needed
'have' does not agree with the singular subject 'Rina'
'will finished' is not correct grammar

solution: Rina has already finished her homework, so she can play now.
'has finished' is the present perfect tense: a past action with a result now.

questions.stem: I ____ a comic when the lights went out.

explain.why: 'am reading' is present, but 'went out' is past
'have read' is present perfect and links to now, but 'went out' is a finished past event
'will read' is future, but 'went out' is past

solution: I was reading a comic when the lights went out.
'was reading' is the past continuous: an action in progress when another happened.

questions.stem: The window ____ by the ball.

explain.why: 'broken' needs 'was' to form the passive
'was breaking' is past continuous, not passive
'broke' is active, but 'by the ball' shows the passive

solution: The window was broken by the ball.
'was broken' is the passive voice: be + past participle.

questions.stem: Mrs Tan ____ our test papers.

explain.why: 'were marked' is passive and plural, but Mrs Tan is the doer and the object 'our test papers' follows
'was marked' is passive, but it cannot take the object 'our test papers' after it
'has been marked' is passive, but it cannot take the object 'our test papers' after it

solution: Mrs Tan marked our test papers.
'marked' is the active voice: the subject does the action.

questions.stem: Yesterday, the cake ____ baked by the cook.

explain.why: 'cake' is singular, so 'were' does not agree
'has baked by' is not correct passive form
'is' is present, but 'Yesterday' is past

solution: Yesterday, the cake was baked by the cook.
'was baked' is the passive: the singular 'cake' takes 'was'.

questions.stem: This bag is ____ than that one.

explain.why: 'heaviest' is the superlative, but 'than' compares two
'heavy' forms its comparative with -ier, not 'more'
-y changes to -i before -er: heavier

solution: This bag is heavier than that one.
'heavier' is the comparative form of 'heavy'.

questions.stem: This is the ____ garden I have ever seen.

explain.why: long adjectives use 'most', not -est
long adjectives use 'most', not -est
'more' is comparative, but 'ever seen' needs the superlative

solution: This is the most beautiful garden I have ever seen.
'most beautiful' is the superlative of the long adjective 'beautiful'.

questions.stem: Please carry the glass ____.

explain.why: 'carefuller' is a comparative adjective
'careful' is an adjective, but an adverb is needed to describe 'carry'
'carefulness' is a noun, so it cannot describe 'carry'

solution: Please carry the glass carefully.
'carefully' is the adverb formed from 'careful'.

questions.stem: Her ____ touched the whole class.

explain.why: 'kindly' is an adverb, but a noun is needed as the subject
'unkind' is an adjective, but a noun is needed as the subject
'kinder' is a comparative adjective, but a noun is needed

solution: Her kindness touched the whole class.
'kindness' is an abstract noun: it names a quality.

questions.stem: A ____ of bees flew over the playground.

explain.why: a 'pack' is a group of wolves or dogs
a 'fleet' is a group of ships
a 'herd' is a group of cattle, not bees

solution: A swarm of bees flew over the playground.
'swarm' is the collective noun for bees.

questions.stem: The books on the table ____ mine.

explain.why: 'books' is plural, so 'is' does not agree
'be' cannot follow a plural subject here
'am' is used only with 'I'

solution: The books on the table are mine.
'books' is plural, so the verb is 'are'.

questions.stem: Mr Lim gave Amy and ____ some advice.

explain.why: 'I' is a subject pronoun, but 'gave Amy and ____' needs an object pronoun
'mine' is a possessive pronoun
'myself' is reflexive and the action is not done to oneself

solution: Mr Lim gave Amy and me some advice.
'me' is the object pronoun, as it receives the advice.

questions.stem: That seat is ____.

explain.why: 'my' must be followed by a noun
'I' is a subject pronoun and does not show ownership
'myself' is a reflexive pronoun and cannot show that the seat belongs to me

solution: That seat is mine.
'mine' is a possessive pronoun: it stands alone.

questions.stem: The cat jumped ____ the sofa.

explain.why: 'and' is a conjunction and cannot show where the cat jumped
'softly' is an adverb and cannot link 'jumped' to 'the sofa'
'quickly' is an adverb and cannot link 'jumped' to 'the sofa'

solution: The cat jumped onto the sofa.
'onto' is a preposition: it links the verb to the noun and shows direction.

questions.stem: Dad goes for a ____ every morning.

explain.why: 'to run' is a verb form, but a noun is needed after 'a'
'ran' is a past verb, but a noun is needed after 'a'
'a runs' is wrong; 'a' needs a singular noun

solution: Dad goes for a run every morning.
'run' is a noun here: 'a run' means a jog.

questions.stem: You must ____ your badge in school.

explain.why: after the modal 'must', the base verb is needed, not the past form
after the modal 'must', the base verb is needed, not the -s form
after the modal 'must', the base verb is needed, not the -ing form

solution: You must wear your badge in school.
'must' is a modal verb: it is followed by the base verb 'wear'.

questions.stem: The pupils waited ____ the bell rang.

explain.why: 'during' is a preposition and needs a noun, not a clause
'beside' is a preposition and needs a noun, not a clause
'towards' is a preposition and needs a noun, not a clause

solution: The pupils waited until the bell rang.
'until' is a conjunction: it introduces the clause 'the bell rang'.

questions.stem: By the time the bell rang, I ____ my lunch.

explain.why: 'have finished' is present perfect, but 'rang' is past
'am finishing' is present, but 'rang' is past
'will finish' is future, but 'rang' is past

solution: By the time the bell rang, I had finished my lunch.
'had finished' is the past perfect: an action completed before another past action.

questions.stem: Ali studied hard every night, ____ he did not pass the test.

explain.why: 'if' gives a condition, but nothing depends on a condition here and it cannot show the contrast needed
'so' shows a result, but not passing is the opposite of what is expected
'because' gives a reason, but hard study is not the reason for failing

solution: Ali studied hard every night, but he did not pass the test.
'but' is a conjunction showing contrast between the two clauses.

questions.stem: The match was cancelled ____ it rained heavily.

explain.why: 'until' shows time, not a reason
'unless' gives a condition, not a reason
'although' shows contrast, but the rain is the reason

solution: The match was cancelled because it rained heavily.
'because' is a conjunction giving the reason.

questions.stem: We will go to the park ____ it stops raining.

explain.why: 'unless' means 'if not', which reverses the meaning
'although' shows contrast, but this is a condition
'because' gives a reason, but the rain has not stopped yet

solution: We will go to the park if it stops raining.
'if' is a conjunction introducing a condition.

questions.stem: Mum said ____ dinner was ready.

explain.why: 'who' refers to a person
'to' is a preposition and cannot introduce what Mum said
'whom' refers to a person as an object

solution: Mum said that dinner was ready.
'that' is a conjunction joining 'Mum said' to what she said.

questions.stem: Please finish your work ____ the bell rings.

explain.why: 'beside' is a preposition and shows position
'during' is a preposition and cannot join a clause
'under' is a preposition and shows position

solution: Please finish your work before the bell rings.
'before' is a conjunction introducing the clause 'the bell rings'.

questions.stem: We have lived here ____ 2015.

explain.why: 'during' does not fit with the perfect tense and a year
'because' is a conjunction and does not fit before a year
'for' is used with a length of time, not a starting point

solution: We have lived here since 2015.
'since' is a preposition giving the starting point.

questions.stem: The box of pencils ____ on the desk.

explain.why: the subject is 'box', not 'pencils'
the subject is 'box', so 'are' does not agree
'be' is the base form and cannot be the verb after the singular subject 'box'

solution: The box of pencils was on the desk.
The head noun 'box' is singular, so the verb is 'was'.

questions.stem: The leader of the two teams ____ waiting at the gate.

explain.why: 'have been' is plural
'leader' is singular, so 'were' does not agree
'leader' is singular, so 'are' does not agree

solution: The leader of the two teams was waiting at the gate.
The head noun 'leader' is singular, so the verb is 'was'.

questions.stem: Mrs Lim gave ____ a surprise quiz.

explain.why: 'we' is a subject pronoun, but the receiver needs the object form
'our' is possessive and needs a noun after it
'ours' is a possessive pronoun and does not fit here

solution: Mrs Lim gave us a surprise quiz.
'us' is the object pronoun receiving the quiz.

questions.stem: The vase was knocked over ____ the puppy.

explain.why: 'with' would make the puppy a tool or companion, but the doer in a passive sentence is introduced by 'by'
the passive agent is introduced by 'by'
the passive agent is introduced by 'by'

solution: The vase was knocked over by the puppy.
'by' introduces the doer in a passive sentence.

questions.stem: The gate was ____ by the caretaker at six.

explain.why: 'locking' is a present participle
after 'was', the past participle is needed
'locks' is simple present

solution: The gate was locked by the caretaker at six.
'was locked' is the passive voice: be + past participle.

questions.stem: The roof has ____ repaired by the school.

explain.why: 'has being' is wrong: 'has' needs the past participle 'been'
'has was' is wrong: 'has' needs the past participle 'been'
'has be' is wrong: 'has' needs the past participle 'been'

solution: The roof has been repaired by the school.
'has been repaired' is the passive in the present perfect.

questions.stem: Although it was raining, the pupils ____ on the field trip.

explain.why: 'gone' needs a helping verb
'to go' is not a finished verb
'going' is not a finished verb

solution: Although it was raining, the pupils went on the field trip.
'went' is the verb of the main clause: it can stand alone.

questions.stem: We stayed indoors ____ the haze was thick.

explain.why: 'so' shows a result, but the haze is the reason
'however' is an adverb and cannot join clauses
'but' shows contrast

solution: We stayed indoors because the haze was thick.
'because the haze was thick' is the subordinate clause.

questions.stem: The shelter was small, but the children waited under ____.

explain.why: 'he' is a subject pronoun and cannot follow a preposition
'they' is a subject pronoun, but a preposition needs an object pronoun
'its' is a possessive and needs a noun after it

solution: The shelter was small, but the children waited under it.
'under it' is a prepositional phrase: a preposition and an object.

questions.stem: The soup was ____ hot.

explain.why: 'extremer' is not a word
'extremity' is a noun
'extreme' is an adjective, but an adverb is needed to describe 'hot'

solution: The soup was extremely hot.
'extremely' is an adverb that describes the adjective 'hot'.

questions.stem: Mum bought a ____ jacket for the trip.

explain.why: 'lightly' is an adverb, not an adjective
'lighten' is a verb
'lights' is a plural noun

solution: Mum bought a light jacket for the trip.
'light' is an adjective describing the noun 'jacket'.

questions.stem: We took the ____ train to school.

explain.why: 'earl' is a noun, so it cannot describe 'train'
'earliness' is a noun
'earlily' is not a word

solution: We took the early train to school.
